title: [Cloudflare] Adapting to AI penetration testing orchestrators: The Modern Security Model
summary: Over the last month, the number of Large Language Model (LLM) penetration testing and orchestration frameworks has exploded. Just a few weeks ago, ARTEX — an open source agentic penetration testing system that automates offensive security workflows — was the only framework available. In just the last three days, we have seen over 50 framework families attempt to scan Cloudflare customers globally. The number of Internet Protocol (IP) addresses seen running these frameworks has grown into the thousands and continues to increase daily. The proliferation of these frameworks has significantly changed the status quo in cyber defense: defenders are struggling to keep up with the volumetric nature of these autonomously guided attacks.ARTEX was taken down by its creator Autumn-27 on October 8. (“The malicious exploitation of this tool runs entirely counter to its original intent,” they wrote in Chinese.) But in the month since, the ecosystem has exploded with new fragmented versions of it. There are now over 12,000 repositories, with several hundred unique forks containing lineage from the original repository. Additionally, hundreds of other similar agentic orchestration frameworks have been created since October 8. Daily requests of AI penetration testing (pentesting) and exploitation tools has grown by 30x since October 1. These tools have also begun chaining stolen customer credentials in some of the more complex attacks, such as lateral movement chaining throughout an environment.We expect these frameworks to continue to proliferate, and every organization should be prepared to address this threat. To counter LLM-based pentest frameworks, we recommend that all organizations adopt what we call the Modern Security Model, which has six key pillars:Fortify the front gate: Implement a Web Application Firewall (WAF) with advanced rules such as rate limits.Security station in the foyer: Anomaly detection on all web applications your customers access.Identify phony visitors: Implement Bot Defense.Remove the back door: Implement Identity-Gated Access for all high-risk external and internal web applications.Inspect deliveries: Enforce validated schemas and explicit security controls.Neighborhood watch: Implement Threat Intelligence to gain visibility into attacks.What is an LLM penetration and exploitation orchestrator?Open-source pentesting frameworks are able to orchestrate AI agents to carry out stages of the traditional Cyber Kill Chain at scale. Tools like ARTEX have the ability to quickly plug in existing Model Context Protocol (MCP) and connect traditional standalone pentesting tools in novel ways. Some even allow operator direction on what type of task to accomplish. These tools can map and enumerate environments, both from the inside and outside. ARTEX and its forks map assets and environments onto a graph, allowing multiple independent parallel agents to enumerate, verify, prototype, and attack at the speed of inference. These tools turn compromises into a hill-climbable problem, which agents are specifically good at.The AI LLM pentesting tools that currently existWe are currently tracking 50+ AI LLM agents. The table below shows the top five LLM penetration and exploitation orchestrators. Each is extremely popular (1k+ GitHub stars) and fully autonomous. The fully autonomous nature of these agents represents a doctrinal shift in offensive cyber capabilities:Human skills are no longer the limit: A harness performs every step of the OODA loop by observing the environment, orienting itself to prioritize valuable and/or vulnerable targets, decide on an action, and act autonomously.Speed increase: Having multiple parallel agents working towards a goal is a large shift compared to single operator or multiple operator augmented by AI.Scale: A single operator can target multiple organizations at the same time, greatly increasing their blast radius.Small mistakes are easily discovered: Autonomous frameworks relentlessly and systematically test exposed services, including their configurations.ArchitecturePlanning modelBuilt-in capabilities/execution environmentPost-exploitation capabilitiesARTEX (and forks)Planner and parallel agentsGraph of goals, leads, and findings is linked to separate asset graph of targetDirectly on host or container with network/root access, can install/develop tools as neededNothing built-in, requires user instructionLuaN1aoAgentSupervisor agent, planner agent, and generic executor agentsThree graphs, with goals/tasks/blockers, evidence/hypothesises/exploits, and target/localContainer with network/user access, can develop tools as needed and install user packagesBuilt-in SSH and Chisel for tunneling and attempted reconnection after disruptionDecepticonOrchestrator agent dispatching specialist sub-agentsGraph of objectives with prerequisitesKali container running as root, can develop tools as neededDedicated post-access, Active Directory and cloud pivoting skillsCairnDispatcher orchestrating work to existing AI harnesses (Codex, Claude Code, Pi)Graph of facts and leads; new nodes trigger dispatcherKali container with root access or directly on host, can develop tools as neededPrompt guidance and Kali toolsPentestGPT-AgentSupervisor agent and one generic executor agentTask list with dependencies, goals, and evidenceRun on host, can develop tools as neededNothing built-in, requires user instructionObservations from the world's largest networkAs of November 12, ARTEX and its forks make up over 60% of currently known AI penetration testing orchestrators. The charts below help us understand how adoption of these tools has changed over the past six weeks. Since the removal of the original ARTEX repository on October 8, traffic has grown more than tenfold, and has increased more than 30x since October 1.As demonstrated above, the takedown of ARTEX on October 8 (and widespread reporting of it) likely caused a hydra effect, where the removal of the original repository led to a massive increase in the number of forks and modifications which can be seen in the steep acceleration of unique instances around October 8.Identity-chained LLM exploitationOver the last eight weeks, our Cloudforce One team has been called into multiple incident response investigations involving ARTEX and ARTEX-derived LLM exploitation frameworks. We’ve seen firsthand how exposed credentials are being chained with LLM-based exploitation frameworks to gain the upper hand over defenders.We observed multiple incidents in which a threat actor gained initial access to a hyperscaler environment and pivoted directly into the customer's Cloudflare environment. Root-cause analysis revealed a common credential hygiene failure. Attackers repeatedly compromised static, non-expiring tokens running inside CI/CD pipelines, which granted broad, cross-environment access across the organization's hyperscaler infrastructure. LLM frameworks greatly expand the likelihood of a client’s API key being laterally leveraged to take over other tenant environments.ARTEX in actionAs part of one incident response investigation, our team observed ARTEX gaining access to a compromised account-level API token previously used for CI/CD with no IP restrictions or rate limiting. Available evidence indicated that the compromise most likely originated through a third-party hyperscaler.We observed that a large number of new Worker scripts had been created with distinct names such as artex-*, artex-pgrecon-*, artex-pgw-*, and artex-do-*. The naming of each Worker script correlated to distinct behaviors and actions it was taking, and was often postfixed by an alphanumeric identifier. We observed activity in excess of 69 requests per minute across multiple unique parts of their Cloudflare infrastructure and 400 database dump requests in an hour. We also observed attempted persistence mechanisms and attempts to validate session tokens for other third-party applications. While we believe that much of this activity was lightly guided by the human operator, this is just one example of the speed and breadth that ARTEX and similar frameworks can achieve post-compromise.Our recommendation: the Modern Security ModelLarge Language Models increase the ability of a threat actor to rapidly iterate through the Cyber Kill Chain against a target. They do this by giving the actor the advantage of speed and validation. Each step of the Cyber Kill Chain can be validated and fed into the next stage of the attack. This level of orchestration is unparalleled and effectively vaporizes legacy cyber security models. A modern model must be used against these attacks.To help explain this model further, let’s use the metaphor of protecting a house on an estate. Each section below outlines how to defend against the threat at each step.Fortify the front gate: implement traffic control and a WAF with advanced rulesBefore anyone even sets foot on your lawn, they have to reach the perimeter fence.On an unprotected estate, an adversary can drive an endless fleet of decoy trucks straight into your driveway, completely blocking the entrance and smashing through the barriers (Layer 3/4 volumetric floods and direct IP probing).With perimeter gate security in place, all incoming traffic is routed through massive, distributed outer gates miles away from the main house. Rogue delivery trucks are filtered out to the highway, rogue utility tunnels trying to wiretap your property are severed, and only legitimate foot traffic ever reaches your home address.Network traffic control serves as an important role in stopping volumetric attacks.A security station in the foyer: anomaly detectionOnce visitors arrive at the main entry, they meet a strict security station at the foyer.Automated prowlers don't just kick the door; they disguise themselves. They attempt weird ways to get in the door — stuffing paper into the lock, trying variations like //front-door//back-room/ to trick the mechanism into swinging open.The security guard at the door enforces clear rules:You cannot knock 500 times in five seconds.You cannot disguise your path with trickery.You cannot attempt to roll a massive flatbed cart through the front hall to haul away the house's internal blueprints (diagnostic heap dumps). Suspicious behavior is turned away immediately.Implement security keys and hardware based FIDO keys.Web Application Firewall (WAF) serves as a key defense mechanism in stopping application exploitation through rate limits and anomaly detection.Identify phony visitors: implement Bot DefenseA sophisticated intruder rarely looks like a masked burglar; they disguise themselves as ordinary visitors. But automated agents, headless browser scrapers, and AI reconnaissance tools don't act like real people.They don't blink, their posture is unnervingly rigid, their cadence is mechanical, and their "identification" is often a sloppy imitation of a real visitor badge.Bot Defense and challenges act as behavioral specialists watching the crowd through one-way glass. It flags the unnatural cadence, catches the synthetic micro-behaviors, and quietly escorts the machines off the property before they can touch a single doorknob.Remove the back door: implement Identity-Gated Access and micro-segmentationMany homes historically were built with side doors or a cellar hatch (internal admin panels, /actuator diagnostic endpoints, and remote gateways). Even if locked, a prowler could stand on the sidewalk, shine a flashlight on the cellar door, and start picking the lock.Zero Trust application access does something radical: it bricks up the doorway from the outside and restricts which rooms can be entered.To anyone wandering the perimeter, the cellar door does not exist. There is no lock to pick, no handle to rattle, and no light on inside. The only way in is with an escort who checks your biometric badge, confirms your device has a clean bill of health, and steps you directly into the specific room you need — leaving the rest of the house out of view.For those who do enter, you have to ensure they cannot breach rooms next to the room they enter. Micro-segmentation is a highly effective strategy at stopping lateral movement. It limits compromised credentials from breaching production, test, and development systems.Inspect deliveries: enforce validated schemas and explicit security controlsYou receive daily supply deliveries to your estate — groceries, mail, maintenance parts. In digital terms, this is your incoming API traffic, which must be inspected and verified.Intruders often attempt to bypass controls by sending unvalidated payloads or forged delivery manifests meant for restricted internal systems.The porch protocol mandates thorough inspection and schema validation for all traffic:Every incoming request must undergo OpenAPI schema validation to ensure it strictly conforms to expected definitions and structures.Drivers and couriers must present validated mutual TLS (mTLS) certificates to establish trusted, authenticated connections.Any request failing inspection or missing valid credentials is rejected immediately at the boundary.Default-Deny Posture: Every positive security implementation ends with an explicit deny-all rule at the bottom of the ruleset.Neighborhood watch: implement threat intelligence to gain visibility into attacksEven with ironclad walls, an isolated property can be vulnerable if a syndicate invents a brand-new infiltration technique across town.Threat intelligence acts as your warning network with neighboring estates. When a rogue actor sets up a new command-and-control safehouse down the road or begins deploying dynamic tunneling vans in your district, you receive an early dossier. Your estate updates its watchlists, recalibrates its sensors, and slams the gate shut before the actor ever turns onto your street.How to get real-time helpARTEX and similar LLM-based frameworks pose a significant challenge to legacy cyber defense models. Even the historical defense-in-depth model — which emphasizes a classic network DMZ — falls short in today's complex architectures. Tomorrow's attacks will only advance as orchestration tools become the new normal.Securing legacy equipment and on-premises devices requires an identity-gated approach that logically makes these devices impossible to reach on the Internet. Beyond identity, slowing or making lateral movement more noisy is the goal of micro-segmentation. This architecture emphasizes a containment-first approach to security, which is essential when users are consistently losing their keys. When combined, the elements of the Modern Security Model are the answer to this vexing problem.If you are facing an active security incident and need the Cloudforce One team on the ground to help respond to the incident or require threat intelligence support, please contact us immediately. If you need help implementing the Modern Security Model outlined here, please contact our Solutions Engineering team.

title: [HashiCorp] From insight to action: improving infrastructure risk posture with Terraform and Concert
summary: Advances in AI are accelerating vulnerability discovery, uncovering previously unknown weaknesses and complex attack paths. Anthropic’s Claude Mythos cyber reasoning marked a major shift in the vulnerability landscape, demonstrating how frontier AI can identify vulnerabilities that have persisted through traditional testing and expert review. As discovery becomes faster and more sophisticated, organizations will face an even greater volume of findings to assess and prioritize. But finding more vulnerabilities is only the first step. To meaningfully reduce risk, teams need a way to determine which vulnerabilities matter most and a repeatable way to take action to address them. For many organizations, that path from detection to resolution remains fragmented. Disconnected workflows, manual handoffs, and complex infrastructure environments make it difficult to understand what is affected, whether a vulnerability can actually be exploited, and what changes are needed to resolve it. Until teams can turn those insights into action, vulnerabilities remain unresolved and organizations remain exposed. Improving infrastructure risk posture requires connecting vulnerability intelligence with the infrastructure context and governed workflows needed to act. In this blog, we’ll explore how Terraform and IBM Concert help organizations move from insight to action, connecting vulnerability intelligence, infrastructure context, and policy-driven governance as part of IBM’s infrastructure lifecycle management solution. The foundation for infrastructure context and governed action Before organizations can respond consistently to changing requirements, emerging vulnerabilities, or new operational needs, they need a trusted and repeatable way to make infrastructure changes. Without a common workflow for planning, reviewing, and applying these changes, organizations can struggle to translate decisions into safe, consistent action at scale. IBM Terraform has long served as the trusted foundation for defining, provisioning, and managing infrastructure as code throughout its lifecycle. By standardizing infrastructure changes through repeatable workflows, Terraform helps organizations establish a consistent operating model across increasingly complex hybrid cloud environments. At the core of Terraform’s value is the infrastructure context and governed execution it provides. Terraform configuration and state give teams a shared understanding of the infrastructure they manage, while capabilities like Infragraph extend that context into a shared substrate across IBM’s infrastructure portfolio. Accurate, timely context helps teams and agents understand what infrastructure exists, how resources are connected, and where changes may have downstream impact. Equally as important, Terraform provides the governed execution layer for acting on that context. Organizations can codify security, compliance, and operational requirements with policy as code, evaluate proposed changes against those requirements, and embed approvals and controls directly into their infrastructure workflows. Together, infrastructure context and policy-driven governance provide the foundation for controlled action at scale. These workflows become especially powerful when paired with vulnerability intelligence, creating a throughline from vulnerability discovery and prioritization to safe remediation. From vulnerability discovery to prioritized remediation As vulnerability discovery accelerates, teams are under increasing pressure to separate the findings that matter most from the noise and act before exposure turns into impact. The challenge is not simply finding more vulnerabilities, but understanding which ones can actually be exploited and determining what needs to be addressed first. IBM Concert Protect helps teams make that distinction, moving from discovery to evidence-based prioritization: Discover: IBM plans to bring Anthropic’s Claude Mythos cyber reasoning into IBM Concert Protect, extending discovery to previously unknown vulnerabilities, including weaknesses without existing signatures or CVE records. Mythos-powered findings are planned to enter Concert Protect alongside traditional scanner results, helping organizations expand what they can uncover without creating another disconnected source of findings. Validate: With capabilities such as Concert’s proof of exploitability, teams can determine which findings represent real-world exposure. Rather than relying solely on severity scores or exploitability predictions, the capability continuously correlates application, infrastructure, runtime, identity, network and business context to validate whether a vulnerability can actually be exploited within a customer’s environment. Remediate: Once teams understand what needs to be addressed, integrations with Terraform provide a governed path for making the required infrastructure changes. Teams can use established Terraform workflows to plan changes, evaluate them against policy, and execute them consistently across environments. The real value comes from connecting these stages into a unified, consistent vulnerability management workflow. This helps organizations mitigate infrastructure risk more effectively by uncovering more vulnerabilities, validating what matters, and taking action safely at scale. Learn more Together, Terraform and IBM Concert help organizations connect vulnerability discovery and prioritization with the infrastructure context and governed workflows needed to act, creating a more complete approach to improving risk posture across the infrastructure lifecycle. To learn more, join IBM and HashiCorp experts for Rethinking enterprise risk in the AI world on November 19, 2026 at 11 a.m. EST. The 45-minute webinar will explore how advances in AI, including Anthropic’s Claude Mythos, are reshaping vulnerability discovery, how proof of exploitability can help teams determine which risks matter most, and how Terraform can help translate prioritized findings into controlled infrastructure changes. title: [HashiCorp] Secure AI credentials from discovery to remediation with Vault Radar and Vault
summary: AI development may be changing how applications are built, but many of the security problems underneath them are familiar. Applications need credentials to connect to models, cloud services, databases, development tools, and other systems. As teams experiment with new AI services and move applications toward production, those credentials can spread across repositories and development workflows just as other secrets do. An API key gets added to a configuration file to get a prototype running. A developer uses it during testing. The application evolves, the team moves on, but the credential remains. Now the organization has two problems: How do you find credentials that have ended up where they shouldn't be, and once you find them, how do you keep them from ending up there again? That is where secret discovery and secrets management need to come together. AI adds another dimension to secrets sprawl The problem starts well before a credential is compromised. A credential that lives outside an organization's secrets management practices can be difficult to inventory, monitor, and remediate. And simply searching today's code isn't necessarily enough. Credentials can persist in Git history even after they have been removed from the latest version of a file. AI applications often depend on model providers, cloud infrastructure, vector databases, and developer tooling, all of which introduce additional credentials that need to be managed securely. HCP Vault Radar is designed to identify unmanaged secrets throughout development workflows. It scans connected data sources when they're added and as new commits and pull requests are created. Deep scanning can identify secrets in Git history, and supported secret types can include an activeness check to help teams understand which findings demand attention. That applies directly to AI development. Vault Radar currently recognizes multiple OpenAI credentials as built-in secret types, including admin, project, service account, user, and API keys. All five documented OpenAI secret types support activeness checks. The broader default detection library also covers credentials for services such as AWS and Microsoft Azure, which can be part of the infrastructure surrounding an AI application. So imagine that a development team accidentally commits an OpenAI API key to a repository. Discovering it is important but it isn't the end of the story. You found an exposed credential. Now what? Finding a secret tells you where there is a problem but doesn't automatically establish where that credential should live going forward. A team can remove a credential from code, but without changing how the application receives and manages credentials, it's easy to recreate the same problem later. And source code may not be the only place that credential has surfaced. Collaboration platforms such as Confluence, Jira, Slack, and Microsoft Teams sit alongside development workflows, capturing conversations, troubleshooting, and handoffs throughout the build, test, and release lifecycle. Developers may share a credential to solve an immediate problem, only for it to remain in a message, ticket, or project page long after that work is complete. Vault Radar can scan these collaboration environments to help teams identify secrets that may otherwise remain outside traditional code-scanning efforts. Remediation should therefore address more than the individual finding. It should move the credential toward a more consistent management model. HCP Vault Dedicated provides a hosted Vault Enterprise environment for securing, storing, and controlling access to sensitive credentials including tokens, passwords, certificates, and encryption keys. The goal is a simple shift: Instead of applications and developers becoming the places where credentials are managed, Vault becomes the system responsible for managing them. For our hypothetical exposed AI key, the team can first address the compromised credential with the provider and then store the replacement credential in Vault rather than putting it back into source code. From there, the application or AI agent can be updated to retrieve the credential from Vault when it needs it, rather than relying on a secret embedded in corde or configuration. This creates a more durable response to secret exposure. The team hasn't only cleaned up one finding. It has changed how that credential is managed. Keep credentials managed without disrupting application workflows Centralizing a credential raises another practical question: How does an application get the secret it needs? Ideally, applications retrieve secrets through Vault. But that isn't practical for every environment. Vault secrets sync supports environments where secrets need to be available through other secrets managers. Secrets sync keeps Vault as the system of record while synchronizing supported secrets to destinations including AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, Google Cloud Secret Manager, GitHub Repository Actions, and Vercel Projects. That means remediation does not have to end with removing a key from GitHub. A team can replace the exposed credential, bring the new value under management in Vault for centralized visibility and management, and make a supported Vault-managed secret available to applications through the appropriate destination. The application can still get the credential where it needs it without putting the credential back into source code. Instead, the application code can reference the path or variable that points to where the secret is securely stored in Vault, allowing the application to retrieve it when needed rather than embedding the credential itself. Where supported, organizations can also reduce reliance on long-lived credentials by adopting short-lived or dynamically generated credentials through Vault. Turn discovery into a repeatable security practice AI may increase the number and variety of credentials organizations need to manage, but it does not require an entirely new approach to secrets security. The better approach is to connect discovery with management and to find credentials that are exposed, address the immediate exposure, and bring the replacement credential under centralized management with secure, just in time access so the same problem is less likely to happen again. With Vault Radar and Vault, organizations can turn secret discovery from a point-in-time cleanup exercise into part of an ongoing approach to managing credentials as AI development grows. Get started Build a more resilient approach to credential risk. Learn how organizations can move beyond finding exposed secrets to reducing credential risk across the application lifecycle in the credential risk whitepaper. Ready to get started? Explore Vault Radar to see how secret scanning can help uncover unmanaged credentials across development workflows, and HCP Vault Dedicated to learn how those credentials can be brought under centralized secrets management.

title: [Kubernetes] The Shift to cgroup v2 in Kubernetes: What You Need to Know
summary:
In Linux, cgroups (control groups) are a kernel feature used for managing system resources. Kubernetes uses cgroups to allocate resources like CPU and memory to containers, ensuring that applications run smoothly without interfering with each other. With the release of Kubernetes v1.31, support for v1 cgroup management moved into maintenance mode. Support for v2 cgroup management has been stable since Kubernetes v1.25. Compared with cgroup v1, cgroup v2 provides a single unified hierarchy, a more consistent interface, and a stronger foundation for resource isolation and modern resource-management features. Deprecation of cgroup v1Kubernetes has deprecated cgroup v1. Starting with Kubernetes v1.35, failCgroupV1 defaults to true, so the kubelet does not start on a cgroup v1 node by default. Administrators can temporarily set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration file, but removal will follow the Kubernetes deprecation policy. Further removal work is tracked in KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support. If you are still on a release older than v1.35, migrate every Linux node to cgroup v2 before upgrading, or plan to set the temporary failCgroupV1: false override. If you are already on v1.35 or later, confirm that every Linux node runs cgroup v2 (or that you intentionally keep the override). Under the default configuration, a remaining cgroup v1 node fails during kubelet startup. For kubeadm-managed clusters, Kubernetes v1.35 also makes this an earlier, stricter check. The SystemVerification preflight check, provided by k8s.io/system-validators, returns an error during kubeadm init, kubeadm join, and kubeadm upgrade when it detects cgroup v1 with kubelet v1.35 or later; with an older kubelet, the check remains a warning. See kubernetes/system-validators#1.12.1 release notes for details. The top FAQs cover three main areas: why to migrate, the benefits and drawbacks, and key points to keep in mind when using cgroup v2. Limitations of cgroup v1 and Improvements with cgroup v2The Linux kernel documentation describes both interfaces: cgroup v1 documentation cgroup v2 documentation Let's enumerate some known issues. active_file memory is not considered available memoryThe kubelet treats active_file memory as not reclaimable. For I/O-intensive workloads, a large page cache can therefore make the kubelet report memory pressure and evict Pods. This is a known kubelet issue (kubernetes/kubernetes#43916); migrating to cgroup v2 does not by itself change that calculation. The documented workaround is to set equal memory requests and limits for containers that perform intensive I/O, after measuring an appropriate value. Memory QoS updates in Kubernetes v1.36Memory QoS was introduced as an alpha feature in Kubernetes v1.22 and updated in v1.27. It remains alpha in v1.36, but now separates memory throttling from memory reservation and adds tiered memory protection: Memory QoS is available only on Linux nodes that use cgroup v2. It relies on the cgroup v2 memory controller: memory.high provides throttling, while memory.min and memory.low provide hard and soft protection when tiered reservation is enabled. cgroup v1 cannot provide this protection model. Enabling the MemoryQoS feature gate applies memory.high throttling to Burstable containers. The threshold is derived from the request, limit, and memoryThrottlingFactor (default 0.9). memoryReservationPolicy: None is the default. It does not write memory.min or memory.low. memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation maps Guaranteed Pod memory requests to memory.min (hard protection) and Burstable Pod requests to memory.low (soft protection). BestEffort Pods receive neither protection. The kubelet exposes Alpha metrics for the total memory.min and memory.low reservations on a node. Kernel 5.9 or later is recommended. On older kernels, memory.high reclaim can trigger a known livelock; from v1.36 the kubelet logs a warning when Memory QoS is enabled on an affected kernel. For example, to opt in to tiered protection: apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: KubeletConfiguration featureGates: MemoryQoS: true memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation memoryThrottlingFactor: 0.9 The overall Kubernetes recommendation is not to enable Alpha features in production; however, if you judge that memory QoS with tiered reservations is useful for your platform in production, make sure to test the configuration and account for hard-reserved memory before you enable the TieredReservation feature gate. See the Pod QoS documentation for the current mapping of Kubernetes QoS classes to cgroup v2 controls. Container-aware OOM handlingOn cgroup v2 nodes, the kubelet defaults singleProcessOOMKill to false. It therefore sets memory.oom.group for each container cgroup so that an OOM event kills all processes in that container together, rather than leaving a partially functioning multi-process container. Set singleProcessOOMKill: true only if you need the cgroup v1-compatible behavior where the kernel may kill one process at a time. See the KubeletConfiguration reference for this setting. This behavior is scoped to a container cgroup, not the whole Pod. Also, cgroup.kill is a separate administrative interface: writing 1 to it sends SIGKILL to every process in that cgroup and its descendants; it does not configure OOM behavior. The cgroup v2 memory controller additionally provides memory.events counters that monitoring systems and userspace OOM managers can observe. Rootless supportIn cgroup v1, delegating controllers to less privileged containers may be dangerous. Unlike cgroup v1, cgroup v2 officially supports delegation. Most implementations of rootless containers rely on systemd for delegating v2 controllers to non-root users. This delegation mechanism is separate from Kubernetes Pod user namespaces, which map container users to unprivileged host users. Pod user namespace support graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.36; check its filesystem, kernel, CRI runtime, and OCI runtime prerequisites before enabling it. What else? eBPF stories: In cgroup v1, device access controls are exposed through interface files. The cgroup v2 device controller has no interface files, and is implemented on top of cgroup BPF. Cilium attaches BPF cgroup programs for socket-based load balancing. Its default cgroup root is /run/cilium/cgroupv2. Pressure Stall Information (PSI) reports CPU, memory, and I/O contention at node, Pod, and container level. On supported clusters, the kubelet exposes PSI by default (KubeletPSI is stable and locked on). PSI requires cgroup v2, Linux 4.20 or later, CONFIG_PSI=y, and a kernel not booted with psi=0. The kubelet surfaces the data through the Summary API and /metrics/cadvisor. When migrating, update software that reads the cgroup filesystem directly. The migration guidance recommends cAdvisor v0.43.0 or later and lists compatible Java, Node.js, and automaxprocs versions. CPU weight conversion in newer OCI runtimescgroup v1 uses cpu.shares, whereas cgroup v2 uses cpu.weight. Newer OCI runtimes use an improved non-linear conversion that preserves the default priority and gives small CPU requests more usable granularity. The change is implemented in the OCI runtime rather than Kubernetes: it is available in crun v1.23 and runc v1.3.2. After upgrading a runtime, monitoring or policy tools that predict exact cpu.weight values may need updates. Read New Conversion from cgroup v1 CPU Shares to v2 CPU Weight for the formula, examples, and compatibility considerations. In-place resource updatesIn-place Pod vertical scaling graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.35. Kubernetes v1.36 then  (/blog/2026/04/30/kubernetes-v1-36-inplace-pod-level-resources-beta/) in-place vertical scaling for Pod-level resources by default, as a Beta feature. The kubelet coordinates changes between the Pod-level and container cgroups so that increases create headroom before container limits grow, while decreases constrain containers before shrinking the Pod-level boundary. Accurate aggregate enforcement for this v1.36 feature requires cgroup v2. Adopting cgroup version 2RequirementsHere's what you need to use cgroup v2 with Kubernetes. First up, you need to be using a version of Kubernetes with support for v2 cgroup management; that's been stable since Kubernetes v1.25 and all supported Kubernetes releases include this support. You need at least one Linux node; cgroup is a Linux-only concept Your OS install must run with cgroup v2 enabled The kernel version must be 5.8 or later (5.9 or later is recommended when using memory QoS) The container runtime must support cgroup v2. For example: containerd v1.4 or later supports cgroup v2; use containerd v2.0 or later for automatic cgroup-driver discovery CRI-O v1.20 or later The kubelet and the container runtime must both be configured to use the correct cgroup driver. See Configure the kubelet's cgroup driver to match the container runtime cgroup driver. For now, you can opt back in to use cgroup v1; the Kubernetes project recommends using cgroup v2, but in Kubernetes 1.36 (the current release) the cgroup v1 option remains supported as a fallback. That fallback is scheduled for removal in Kubernetes v1.38. If you are running an older cluster, plan to migrate; if you are setting up a new cluster with Linux nodes, you should prefer cgroup v2. In either case, review both the Kubernetes runtime documentation and (if relevant) the containerd compatibility matrix. kernel updates around cgroup v2When Kubernetes was first announced, in 2014, only v1 cgroup existed. Version 2 cgroup management first appeared in Linux kernel 4.5, released in 2016. In Linux 4.5, the cgroup v2 io, memory, and pids controllers were supported. Linux 4.15 added support for the cgroup v2 cpu controller. Pressure Stall Information (PSI) support began with Linux 4.20. The Kubernetes project does not recommend using cgroup v2 with a Linux kernel older than 5.2 due to lack of cgroup-level task freezer support. Kubernetes documents 5.8 as the minimum kernel version for cgroup v2; the root cgroup's system-level cpu.stat file was added in Linux 5.8. The memory.high livelock fix used by Memory QoS is present in Linux 5.9 and later. memory.peak was added in Linux 5.19. cgroup driver configurationConfigure the kubelet's cgroup driver to match the container runtime cgroup driver. If you use kubeadm to manage your cluster, Kubernetes recommends that you use the systemd cgroup driver, because kubeadm manages the kubelet as a systemd service. For other management tooling, check the documentation for the tool you're using to manage your cluster. If you can pick either option, I recommend using the systemd driver. Whatever tooling you've chosen, the kubelet automatically tries to detect the runtime's recommended cgroup driver. This automatic detection relies on using a runtime that implements the RuntimeConfig CRI RPC (for example: containerd v2.0+ or CRI-O v1.28+). If you're using a container runtime that supports cgroup v2 but doesn't support automatic cgroup driver detection, you can manually configure an override by editing the kubelet configuration file. For example: apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: KubeletConfiguration cgroupDriver: systemd Automatic discovery of the runtime's cgroup driver through the CRI, tracked by KEP-4033, graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.34. It requires a runtime that implements the RuntimeConfig CRI RPC (containerd v2.0+ or CRI-O v1.28+). When available, the kubelet uses the value reported by the runtime instead of its configured cgroupDriver value. Tools and commands for troubleshootingTools and commands that you should know about cgroups: stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup/: Check whether cgroup v2 is enabled; it returns cgroup2fs. systemctl list-units 'kube*' --type=slice or --type=scope: List Kubernetes-related units that systemd currently has in memory. bpftool cgroup list /sys/fs/cgroup/*: List all programs attached to the cgroup CGROUP. systemd-cgls /sys/fs/cgroup/*: Recursively show control group contents. systemd-cgtop: Show top control groups by their resource usage. tree -L 2 -d /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice: Show Pods' related cgroups directories. How to check if a Pod CPU or memory limit is successfully applied to the cgroup file?Work from the API object down to the node. Identify the node, then compare desired resources in the spec with the enacted values in status (in-place resize can leave those out of sync): kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}{"
"}' kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{range .spec.containers}{.name}{" spec	"}{.resources}{"
"}{end}' kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{range .status.containerStatuses}{.name}{" status	"}{.resources}{"
"}{end}' On that node, as root, with the systemd cgroup driver and cgroup v2 (these snippets also need jq). Pin the container with kubelet labels; a container name alone is not unique on a node. Use crictl ps -a if the container is not running: CONTAINER_ID=$(crictl ps \ --label io.kubernetes.pod.namespace=<namespace> \ --label io.kubernetes.pod.name=<pod-name> \ --name <container-name> -q | head -n1) # OCI view (not the CRI protobuf field names) crictl inspect "$CONTAINER_ID" | jq '.info.runtimeSpec.linux.resources' # Kernel cgroup path for this container PID=$(crictl inspect "$CONTAINER_ID" | jq -r '.info.pid') CGROUP="/sys/fs/cgroup$(awk -F: '$1=="0"{print $3}' /proc/$PID/cgroup)" cat "$CGROUP/cpu.weight" # request.cpu → shares → weight; not a limit cat "$CGROUP/cpu.max" # limit.cpu as "quota period"; unlimited is "max <period>" cat "$CGROUP/memory.max" # limit.memory; unlimited is "max" # Pod-level cgroup (parent slice), used by Pod-level resources cat "$(dirname "$CGROUP")/cpu.max" "$(dirname "$CGROUP")/memory.max" # Present when MemoryQoS is enabled cat "$CGROUP/memory.high" "$CGROUP/memory.min" "$CGROUP/memory.low" SCOPE=$(basename "$CGROUP") systemctl show "$SCOPE" \ -p CPUWeight -p CPUQuotaPerSecUSec -p CPUQuotaPeriodUSec -p MemoryMax Do not treat info.runtimeSpec.linux.cgroupsPath as a filesystem path when the runtime uses the systemd driver; that value is a systemd unit path (slice:runtime:id), not a directory under /sys/fs/cgroup. Expected mapping at each layer: Kubernetes: spec.containers.resources (desired) and status.containerStatuses.resources (enacted after in-place resize). Pod-level resources are on spec.resources and the parent pod slice. CRI (kubelet → runtime; these protobuf names stay cgroup v1-style even on v2): cpu_shares, cpu_quota, cpu_period, memory_limit_in_bytes, plus unified for Memory QoS. crictl inspect does not show these names; it shows the OCI spec the runtime derived from them. OCI spec: linux.resources.cpu.{shares,quota,period}, linux.resources.memory.limit, and linux.resources.unified. The runtime converts shares, quota, and period into cgroup v2 files. After upgrading crun or runc, the shares-to-weight formula may change; see CPU weight conversion. systemd scope: CPUWeight, CPUQuotaPerSecUSec, CPUQuotaPeriodUSec, MemoryMax. Unlimited or unset values often appear as  or infinity. cgroupfs: cpu.weight (from CPU request; an unset request still yields the default of 2 shares), cpu.max, and memory.max on the container scope.
