title: [Kubernetes] Scaling Kubernetes Workloads with Node Swap
summary: Memory is often the first hard limit a Kubernetes cluster hits. Nodes run out of RAM long before they run out of CPU, and the new wave of agentic AI workloads makes this worse. These workloads demand large memory footprints to start up and run untrusted code, then sit idle waiting for the next prompt. That idle but resident memory is expensive, and it caps how many pods a node can hold. This is where swap helps. Kubernetes support for running nodes with swap enabled reached General Availability in v1.34, and by backing that swap with fast NVMe solid state drives (SSDs), a node can page out dormant memory and pack in far more pods. This post explains how we benchmarked that approach across three workloads, including CI/CD kernel builds, sandboxed headless browsers, and isolated Python runtimes; we found density gains of up to 3×, often with little or no latency cost. The node density problemThe Kubernetes ecosystem has reached a fundamental physical resource constraint: the strict limits of hardware memory versus the growing demand for dynamic, bursty workloads in the new agentic era. Historically, administrators provisioning memory-intensive workloads encountered a persistent dilemma: set memory limits too high and you waste expensive infrastructure on idle RAM; set them too low and you risk Out-Of-Memory (OOM) kills. This conflict is amplified when deploying autonomous AI agents using secure execution environments like the agent-sandbox framework. These agentic pods require large memory footprints to initialize and execute untrusted code. However, after their burst of activity, they typically enter long-tail idle phases waiting for user prompts. Keeping this idle state in physical RAM caps cluster density and makes AI infrastructure expensive to run. The solution: Kubernetes node swapWith the introduction of Kubernetes' support for running nodes with swap enabled (which reached General Availability in v1.34), this paradigm shifts. By enabling the Linux kernel to page out anonymous memory to disk, node swap acts as a shock absorber during traffic spikes or periods of heavy memory oversubscription. Historically, swap was discouraged in Kubernetes for two reasons. The first was memory accounting. Under cgroup v1, the controls treated memory and swap as a single combined limit rather than letting operators set an independent limit for disk swap. Without independent tracking, a process could page large amounts of anonymous memory out to disk, which made a container's real memory usage unpredictable and hard to isolate. Kubernetes' swap support resolves this by relying on cgroup v2, whose separate swap accounting tracks disk swap on its own. The second reason was the latency penalty of paging to slow spinning disks, which fast NVMe Local SSDs largely eliminate. Together, these make it practical to increase pod density and buffer against memory spikes without sacrificing cluster stability. The benchmark dataTo quantify the performance boundaries and cost-saving potential of Local SSD-backed node swap, this analysis covers three distinct workload categories: a Traditional Build Workload for CI/CD pipelines, High-Density Browser Sandboxes, and Isolated Python Sandboxes. Workload Profile Baseline Capacity (No Swap) Local SSD Swap Capacity Density Improvement Linux CI/CD Kernel Build 600 MB RAM Limit 300 MB RAM Limit -50% RAM Footprint Headless Chrome (Kata) 40 Concurrent Pods 50 Concurrent Pods +25% Pod Density Headless Chrome (gVisor) 80 Concurrent Pods 160 Concurrent Pods +100% Pod Density Python Sandbox (gVisor) 80 Concurrent Pods 240 Concurrent Pods +200% Pod Density 1. Traditional workload: Linux kernel buildBefore exploring specialized agentic architectures, swap was validated against classic batch workloads by running a complete Linux 6.1.1 kernel build. The kernel compilation process leverages concurrent worker threads, balloons in memory to hold compiled object files, and requires a large memory spike during the brief linking phase. This workload mirrors the memory behavior of enterprise CI/CD pipelines. Because earlier compiled objects sit inactive in memory while the pipeline progresses, CI/CD jobs frequently hoard unused physical RAM, which makes them well suited to node swap compression. On a baseline node without swap, the minimum memory limit to prevent an OOM crash during compilation was 600 MB. Routing swap to a Local SSD cut the container memory limit by 50% to 300 MB without incurring any execution slowdown (in fact, it ran cleanly in 374s vs the baseline 433s). However, as an explicit tradeoff, compressing the limit further to 200 MB forced the active working set into swap, causing long I/O wait times and increasing execution time by over 40%. This reinforces that swap serves as an insurance policy for burst memory, not a replacement for active RAM. 2. High-density agent workloads: headless browser runtimesAI agent workloads frequently require manipulating headless browsers via Chromium. However, trusting external code execution often requires stricter security isolation than standard Linux namespaces. This benchmark cross-evaluated several container runtime environments. The raw logs and testing methodologies for the default runtime are available in the Agent Sandbox GKE Swap directory. Unsandboxed baseline limits (runc): To test the limits of the environment without the overhead of security runtimes, plain runc containers were swept on a c4-standard-32 node (32 vCPU, 120 GB RAM). Without swap, the node exhausted physical memory and failed past 512 pods. Enabling Local SSD swap allowed the node to support 768 concurrent pods. Advanced security runtimes (for example: gVisor, Kata Containers): Enabling strict security sandboxing increases memory overhead and normally reduces pod density. However, memory swap naturally absorbs this overhead penalty. Without swap, a gVisor environment hit a hard limit at 80 pods. Local SSD swap doubled that capacity, which allowed 160 concurrent gVisor pods on a single node. Similarly, Kata Containers microVMs exhausted physical RAM at 40 concurrent pods without swap, but using GCP Local SSD swap expanded this to 50 stable Kata microVMs before CPU saturation. At these maximum densities, the per-pod latency increase is driven mainly by pods competing for CPU, not by swap I/O. An operator tuning for a specific latency target would run at a lower density than the peak numbers here and see a proportionally smaller latency cost. For a comprehensive architectural breakdown and density metrics for gVisor and Kata, see the Agent Sandbox GKE Swap Runtimes directory. 3. Beyond browsers: sandboxed Python runtimesThe advantages of node swap also extend to untrusted, isolated code-execution environments. This sweep deployed simultaneous Python sandbox sessions analyzing 5 million rows of data from the MovieLens 20M dataset, requiring a ≃375 MiB resident memory footprint per execution. The in-depth scaling results and deployment code for this sweep can be reviewed in the Agent Sandbox GKE Swap Python Density directory. Without swap, heavy concurrent bursts exhausted physical memory, causing the node to hit a hard RAM limit and fail at 80 concurrent sessions. Enabling Local SSD swap offloaded dormant anonymous memory, freeing up physical RAM and preserving the node's page cache. This allowed the node to scale to 240 concurrently isolated Python sandboxes—a 3× density improvement. As with the browser workloads, the latency rise at peak density comes mainly from the sandboxes competing for CPU rather than from swap itself. Density Benchmarks with and without Node Swap How to use itIf you manage Kubernetes infrastructure for developer environments, browser testing farms, JVM applications, or AI execution runtimes, leveraging Local SSD swap can multiply your density efficiency. In Kubernetes v1.34+, node swap is Generally Available. You enable it via the kubelet configuration: kind: KubeletConfiguration apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 failSwapOn: false memorySwap: swapBehavior: LimitedSwap Pairing this upstream configuration with your cloud provider's high-speed local disk gives you dynamic memory balancing. For example, this is natively supported on Google Kubernetes Engine via Node Memory Swap configured on Local SSD profiles. To get the benefits, configure your workloads with Burstable QoS: set your container's memory limits higher than its requests. The node automatically rations fast swap space based on idle application memory usage while keeping active processes responsive. ConclusionAs the Kubernetes ecosystem transitions into the agentic era, administrators face a growing conflict between finite hardware memory limits and the bursty behavior of AI workloads. Frameworks like Agent Sandbox provide the security isolation required for running untrusted agents, but that isolation traditionally demands large amounts of idle memory overhead. By configuring the kubelet with LimitedSwap and routing it to Local SSDs, you can mitigate this conflict. Fast swap offloads the dormant states of idle agents, allowing you to increase pod density and node utilization on the same infrastructure without compromising security boundaries.

title: [Cloudflare] Kitesurf is now open source
summary: We introduced Kitesurf, our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to.That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers.A browser built for agentsKitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer.Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network.Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial announcement and how to use it in Browser Run’s developer documentation.What is inside the repository?Kitesurf builds on Cloudflare’s Developer Platform and APIs, alongside an ecosystem of open-source Rust packages compiled to WebAssembly:Blitz provides HTML parsing, the DOM, layout, and painting.Stylo provides CSS parsing, cascading, and computed styles.Boa runs JavaScript inside WebAssembly (as the last resort only when we can’t run JavaScript in Dynamic Workers).Linebender libraries provide text layout and 2D graphics, and Krilla generates PDF output.These projects made Kitesurf possible. They retain their respective licenses; the repository's NOTICE documents third-party notices.Kitesurf has three main parts: the Engine manages browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer draws the result.All packages, the engine, its Rust core, DOM shims, renderer, and Kitesurf CLI live separately in folders under the repository’s packages directory where you can explore how all the pieces fit together.Run your own KitesurfTo run Kitesurf locally, follow the repository's build requirements, then clone the repository, install dependencies, and start the engine:git clone https://github.com/cloudflare/kitesurf.git cd kitesurf pnpm install --frozen-lockfile pnpm run devThe first build compiles the Rust core and its dependencies, so give it some time. Subsequent builds reuse the build cache. Finally wrangler starts a local development server at http://127.0.0.1:8787. Open that address to try a page in Chrome DevTools, or use it programmatically.You can use puppeteer with a NodeJS script:import puppeteer from "puppeteer-core"; const browser = await puppeteer.connect({ browserWSEndpoint: "ws://127.0.0.1:8787/devtools/browser", }); try { const page = await browser.newPage(); await page.goto("https://example.com/"); await page.screenshot({ path: "page.png" }); } finally { await browser.disconnect(); }Or you can point your AI harness at the local CDP port (agents love CDP) and watch it take full control of Kitesurf.Deploy to your Cloudflare accountWhen you’re done changing and testing locally, you can deploy the engine to your own account and use Kitesurf from there instead of the Browser Run managed APIs we provide. Note that a Workers Paid plan is required because Kitesurf uses Dynamic Workers to create isolated Workers for pages.From the repository root:pnpm run deployHelp us make it betterAs with all of our open-sourced projects, Kitesurf lives in Github and we welcome forks and contributions. However, note that Kitesurf is under heavy development and we are focusing on making the engine more compatible (check out Web Platform Test evolution), more reliable, and efficient.Start with the contribution guidelines if you want to contribute. Open an issue with a minimal reproduction or a proposed approach, and get vouched by a maintainer before opening a pull request. Focused fixes with tests, clear evidence, and a well-defined scope are much easier to review than large rewrites or unrelated cleanup, but all contribution does not have to be code: a small page that reproduces a rendering bug, a failing automation workflow, or a clear documentation correction can help us move forward.Stay tunedKitesurf is evolving quickly. Stay tuned for updates in the blog and our changelog, and keep an eye on the official landing page for the latest on standards compatibility in Web Platform Tests page and benchmarks.And come chat with the team on Discord. We’re building a browser for agents, and we’d love your help making it better.

title: [Cloudflare] Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithm
summary: Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat, an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm published by researchers Tennage & Băsescu et al. called QuePaxa (2023). QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well.Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat.Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works.What we’re building and why it’s uniqueMeerkat is a distributed system in which replicas agree upon an ordered log of events, where each event is decided by a consensus algorithm.Consensus algorithms allow a group of machines to agree on a single shared truth, even if some of those machines crash or disconnect. Consensus algorithms provide an important guarantee: machines never decide conflicting values. This ensures Meerkat replicas’ logs never diverge.Meerkat uses its consensus-powered log to expose applications like a key-value store, where each entry in the log is a get or a put. Because the consensus algorithm guarantees replicas’ logs never diverge, they all construct the same key-value (KV) state. Comparable consensus-powered systems include Consul, etcd, and Apache ZooKeeper.Unlike similar systems, however, Meerkat was designed for global scale. A Meerkat cluster may be distributed across continents and connected by links that often exhibit high and variable latency. This is an unusual setup for consensus systems, which are usually deployed in smaller, more local networks, and have strict latency requirements.The challenges of consensus at a global scaleWhile all consensus algorithms ensure that replicas agree on the same value, many of them become disproportionately unavailable or slow when network conditions degrade (but machines do not crash). We have seen this happen firsthand: in 2020, the partial failure of a core Cloudflare network switch caused a consensus-powered system to degrade and the dashboard to operate 80x slower than usual, for six hours. Critically, the system lost no data. But it became unavailable for writes until the issue was resolved, which is unacceptable.Ideally, a consensus algorithm should be able to make progress despite latency spikes and broken connections, not just replica failures. This is particularly a problem at global scale, where faults are more likely to originate in the network, and not our own servers.Let’s examine two common traits of consensus algorithms that can lead to degradation under hostile network conditions: destructive interference and fault detection. Later, we’ll see how QuePaxa sidesteps both of these issues.Destructive interference and leadersConsider Paxos, the veritable grandfather of most consensus algorithms. A lot of consensus algorithms inherit the structure of Paxos – both the good and the not-so-good bits.Leaving an egregious amount of detail out, here’s how Paxos works. There are two kinds of processes: proposers and acceptors. Abstractly, the goal of the system is for a majority of acceptors to agree on a value proposed by some proposer. There are two phases: the Prepare phase, and the Accept phase. In the Prepare phase, any proposer can send a ballot number out to a majority of acceptors. This ballot number serves as a promise – acceptors will only accept proposals with that ballot number or higher. Then, in the Accept phase, the proposer sends its proposal along with the ballot number to a majority of acceptors again. If a majority of acceptors still hold the ballot number of the proposal, the majority accepts it, and the proposer can safely decide the proposal.Challenges arise when two or more proposers submit proposals at the same time. Specifically, another proposer can interleave its own higher ballot number in between the two phases, blocking any lower ballots. Two proposers can repeatedly block each other from progressing – effectively competing for acceptance.When proposers compete and block each other in this way, we say that they destructively interfere. Destructive interference gets worse as more proposers propose their own ballots. The more concurrent proposers there are, the more likely it is that the system gets stuck repeatedly proposing. Even if none of the replicas have crashed or are unavailable, multiple proposers and misbehaving networks can block Paxos. Formally, we say that Paxos does not guarantee liveness (i.e., that proposals are eventually decided) without assuming that, at some point, all messages arrive within a bounded amount of time — an assumption known as partial synchrony.To avoid multiple proposers constantly competing, most deployed consensus algorithms, like Raft, Multi-Paxos, and Viewstamped Replication, add a special leader proposer. The leader is the only replica that can make proposals. Centralizing the proposing power in one replica forces an order on concurrent requests, avoids competing proposals, and has the added benefit of getting decisions done in an optimal single network round-trip, instead of two. While the leader is healthy and the network is well-behaved, leader-based protocols are fast.The trade-off is that the leader must remain operational and reachable. When it fails, becomes too slow, or is disconnected from the cluster, the system stalls. The only solution is for the remaining replicas to detect that the leader has failed, and elect a new one in its place.When leader recovery is unstableWhen a leader fails, the system must recover by electing a new one. Interestingly, leader recovery is often how destructive interference sneaks right back into a leader-based system.Consider Raft. For safety reasons, Raft elects a new leader using a majority vote. A replica that suspects that the leader has failed announces itself as a candidate for leadership and requests a vote from other replicas. If more than half of the replicas agree to vote for the candidate, it becomes the new leader. If they don’t, then a new election is called, and the candidates try again.Multiple replicas can become candidates — all they need to do is detect that the leader is down. The candidates may then all try to acquire a majority vote simultaneously. The problem is that the candidates will compete for the majority vote, which means Raft’s elections suffer from the destructive interference we just saw in Paxos: two replicas can mutually prevent each other from getting support from a majority and becoming the leader. The more elections fail, the more replicas will try to get themselves elected leader.Even if the leader stops being faulty, elections continue to disrupt what could have been normal system functioning. This is known as a metastable failure: a failure pattern that perpetuates itself even when the initial cause of failure is removed. A two-second network outage — or a momentarily faulty network switch — can make the leader appear to be faulty and force a leader election, which can fail, and force further elections. The outage will be over in two seconds, but the election can continue for much longer as candidates continue to block each other.Ideally, consensus algorithms wouldn’t need any recovery process, as they are complicated, prone to interference, and introduce another source of downtime.When fault detection goes awryThe problem of destructive interference in leader elections is compounded by trigger-happy fault-detection, especially in wide-area networks. In order for leader-based consensus algorithms to choose a new leader, replicas must first detect that the leader has failed. However, if replicas detect leader-failures inaccurately, the system may spend an inordinate amount of time in recovery, not handling requests.In a distributed system, where machines are separated over a network, fault detection will ultimately depend on expectations. A process cannot directly observe that a remote process has failed; it can only observe that an expected message has or hasn’t arrived. We need a predictable pattern of communication, such as heartbeats or acknowledgements, to tell us that a machine is healthy. If an expected message does not arrive within the expected time, we suspect a fault. The difficulty lies in managing those expectations.In real networks, especially wide-area networks, messages don’t always arrive when predicted. There is no guaranteed upper bound on the time that it takes for messages to arrive. That’s not to say that the network is slow, or that it is unreliable — most messages arrive within the time we expect them to. Instead, sudden bursts of latency and losses in connectivity can, momentarily, and without warning, increase the time it takes for any message to traverse the network. We call such networks asynchronous.The big issue with asynchronous networks is that if some server doesn’t reply in a given amount of time, we don’t really know if the server has failed or if the network is just slow — the two are indistinguishable over the network. Any practical fault detector has to make a guess based on how long it has been waiting compared to its expectation, and sometimes that guess will be wrong.In leader-based algorithms, that guess is exactly what triggers leader elections. Sometimes the leader is down; sometimes its messages are late, or the connection is silently broken. The protocol cannot know which one happened before it reacts. If the guess is wrong, and a replica thinks the leader is faulty when it actually isn’t, then an election begins and the entire system must stop. Until the leader is replaced, no progress is made — and as we just saw, that can take a while.Fault detection is fundamentally error-prone in asynchronous networks, and when the detector makes a mistake, we get downtime.When fault detection is slowEven when a fault detector guesses correctly, there are issues. Fault detectors react to failures by observing messages on the network, and so their response time has to scale with network latency — the detector’s timeout can’t be below the network latency. This is why Raft is commonly deployed with an election timeout of five to ten times the network round-trip time. It has to be high enough to give a chance for the leader to signal that it is alive, and avoid falsely triggering elections. The election timeout can be much lower than that, but since leader elections completely stop the system, timeouts are usually set conservatively high.Roughly speaking, a round trip halfway across the world is measured in hundreds of milliseconds. If an election timeout is several round trips, detecting a failed coordinator can take around a second. Even when fault detection is completely accurate, it is slow, and it is slowest in high-latency global networks. Until the detector reacts, the system is down.Why QuePaxa is the right fitWe realized that any algorithm relying on a strict leader or accurate timeouts was inevitably going to stall in a consensus system that runs over the Internet. We searched for consensus algorithms designed for asynchronous environments — protocols that didn't rely on a well-behaved network or precise timing to function. This led us to QuePaxa, published in 2023 by Tennage & Băsescu et al.The most notable thing about QuePaxa is how it can efficiently reach consensus in a single round trip under favorable network conditions, but also gracefully degrades performance during latency spikes, connectivity issues, and server failures. QuePaxa achieves this by solving the exact problems we just discussed through three key design choices: having an optional leader, completely removing the reliance on fault detection, and designing for constructive interference between proposers.In QuePaxa, much like in Paxos, there are two roles: proposers and recorders. Proposers submit proposals to be decided on, and recorders serve as intermediaries between proposers, recording every proposal they see.Instead of having proposers compete to get their own proposals decided, in QuePaxa, proposers will cooperatively work towards a proposal that everyone supports. QuePaxa does this by assigning a priority to proposals, in the form of a random number. The optional leader gets an exclusive maximum priority. During execution, proposers submit their proposals to the recorders, who propagate the proposal to other active proposers. When proposers receive a proposal from a recorder with a higher priority than theirs, they adopt the new proposal as their own, i.e., begin broadcasting the higher priority proposal instead. In general, proposers in QuePaxa work together to decide on the highest priority proposal that they collectively know. This means proposers can’t lock each other out of deciding on a proposal, indefinitely.The caveat is that it might not be possible to spread proposals around well enough to agree on a proposal, and so proposers have to try again, with each attempt constituting a round. However, as more proposers submit proposals, the more likely they are to converge on the highest priority proposal. This is what makes QuePaxa a randomized algorithm: the randomly generated priorities of non-leader proposers are likely — but not guaranteed — to lead to consensus on the highest known priority, in a round. Yet, given enough rounds, it is guaranteed that proposers agree on a proposal.One proposer is designated the leader. The leader is the only proposer capable of deciding in a single round trip. The leader always proposes with the highest priority; if the leader knows it spread its proposal before any other proposer, then it can decide immediately. Clients aren’t forced to make requests to the leader — any proposer can propose. If the leader goes down, then clients can keep making requests to other proposers. The leader is completely optional. The leader is simply more likely to decide, than any other proposer, and do so faster, in a single round trip.However, because the leader is the only one that can decide in a single round trip, we want to use it whenever possible. To exploit this fast path without creating a single point of failure, clients sending proposals to the system hedge their bets: they send their requests for proposals to every replica, and the non-leader replicas will wait for a small timeout, so the leader can propose and decide on its own. In our own implementation of QuePaxa, we actually deviate from the paper and have clients wait the hedge timeout instead of the replicas, to reduce the amount of messages we send over the network, but the overall result is the same.This hedging timeout is very different from the timeouts used in Raft or Multi-Paxos. It is not fault detection, and so isn’t constrained by network latency; it is locally determined by replicas and can be as small as they want it to be. In Raft, having a five-millisecond timeout in a network with 100-millisecond latency would completely freeze the system. But in QuePaxa, a five-millisecond hedge timeout only increases the number of active proposers.However, hedging isn’t free: the more proposers there are, the more proposals get broadcast, and the more likely it is that replicas fail to decide in a round. Instead, hedging provides a tradeoff: we can react faster to leader changes by lowering the hedge timeout, but we incur extra bandwidth costs and may take more time to decide. That’s a tradeoff we're more than willing to make.If the QuePaxa leader goes down, we can recover as fast as we want — we’re not bound by network latency. This is how QuePaxa gets around fault detection: since anyone can propose, not just the leader, QuePaxa can proactively deal with leader failures by hedging, rather than reacting to failures.How QuePaxa works under the hoodTo understand how QuePaxa gives us all of these nice properties, let’s look at how QuePaxa actually works. QuePaxa works in rounds made up of four phases. If a proposal hasn’t been decided on in the last phase, a new round is started, and QuePaxa starts over. At the start of each phase, proposers broadcast their currently adopted proposal to all recorders. Once a proposer receives a reply from a majority of recorders, they advance to the next phase. Here’s the general outline of the phases:Phase 0 (Propose and Adopt): Proposers randomly select a priority, send their proposals to recorders, and adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority of recorders. If it’s the first round and the leader knows its proposal reached a majority of recorders first, the leader decides immediately.Phase 1 (Spread): Proposers spread their adopted proposal to a majority of recorders.Phase 2 (Check and Decide): Proposers ask a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal seen in the previous phase. If it matches their own adopted proposal, they decide on it.Phase 3 (Carry Forward): Any proposer that failed to decide prepares for the next round by adopting the best proposal they see from a majority of recorders.Let’s walk through a couple of example executions and unpack how each phase contributes to the overall behavior we want out of QuePaxa. Each execution will have two proposers (one of which is the leader) and three recorders.The Leader Fast Path (Phase 0): The first phase does three important things: it randomizes priorities (which it must do to circumvent the FLP impossibility theorem), checks if the leader reached a majority of support first, and helps proposers converge if the leader didn't. The leader’s proposal is not randomized, and will always have the highest possible priority.In the example above, the leader's proposal reaches a majority of recorders before anyone else, and receives replies confirming it. The leader can safely decide right away. This might seem dangerous, but it is entirely safe thanks to a property called majority intersection: any two majorities of recorders always share at least one recorder. Because the leader reached a majority, any other proposer querying a majority will inevitably encounter the leader's proposal and adopt it. Since the leader’s proposal has the highest priority, any other proposer will adopt the leader’s proposal. It is impossible to decide on any other proposal.Concurrent Slow Path (Phases 0-3): When there are concurrent proposers, however, it is not guaranteed that the leader will immediately decide. The leader might fail to reach a majority of recorders first, or it might receive a single reply supporting another proposer. Let's look at what happens when another proposer contests the leader.Phase 0: Pictured below, a second proposer (shown in red) reaches the second and third recorders first. The fast path is blocked. Instead of competing, proposers adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority and move to the second phase. The two proposers could both converge to the leader’s proposal in this phase. For illustrative purposes, our example will prevent convergence by delaying the leader’s messages. Phase 1: Proposers spread the proposal they just adopted in Phase 0 to a majority of recorders. The recorders keep track of the highest-priority proposal they observe. It is a simple but critical step: it prevents the protocol from later deciding on a lower-priority proposal. This is once again thanks to majority intersection: any majority queried in the following phase must include at least one recorder that saw the adopted proposal, in this phase. For illustrative purposes, we prevent convergence in this phase by delaying the leader’s message to the third recorder, so the recorder does not adopt the leader’s proposal.Phase 2: Now, a decision can happen. Each proposer determines if a higher-priority proposal gained enough support to overtake its own by asking a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal observed during Phase 1. If the highest proposal returned is still their adopted proposal, they decide. In our diagram, the leader sees its own proposal returned by a majority and safely decides. The other proposer receives conflicting summaries, so it cannot decide yet. Like in Phase 1, recorders keep track of the highest priority proposal they received.Phase 3: If a proposer doesn’t decide in Phase 2, it moves to the final cleanup phase to prepare for the next round. Proposers spread their proposals again and adopt the best they find among a majority of recorders. Here, the remaining proposer discovers the decided proposal and adopts it, heading into the next round.This is deliberate — if there was some decision in the previous phase, then a majority of the recorders will have that proposal, and any remaining proposers are guaranteed to adopt it. We see here another instance of cooperation between proposers — even when a round fails, proposers try to converge on the same proposal heading into the next round.Moving to the next round: After the fourth phase, proposers move on to the next round. At this point, there is no more leader fast path, and the only way to decide is by converging in the third phase. Importantly, due to proposal adoption, it becomes exponentially easier to decide as rounds progress. The QuePaxa paper predicts that each round has a 50% chance of deciding, but in practice, that probability is much higher, thanks to convergence.Putting all four phases together, we can see where QuePaxa gets its resilience. The first phase gives the leader its one-round-trip fast path. If that fast path fails, random priorities and proposal adoption help proposers converge instead of compete. The second and third phases make it safe to decide, thanks to majority intersection, while the fourth carries what proposers learned into the next round, in case proposers don’t decide.No proposer has to detect that the leader has failed before making progress, and a failed round doesn’t throw away the work already done. When the network behaves, QuePaxa is fast. When it doesn’t, QuePaxa keeps moving.How QuePaxa makes Meerkat possibleIn our own evaluations of Meerkat, where we had servers spanning nearly all continents, we’ve directly experienced the impact that QuePaxa has on the overall performance and availability of the system. Meerkat continuously processes requests, even when the leader crashes, disconnects, or just becomes slow. At no point have we ever seen it completely stall. This is exactly what we wanted.The rate at which Meerkat handles requests has also been generally predictable. Most decisions — upwards of 95% — are made by the leader in the first phase, which keeps our throughput fairly stable. In the instances where a decision isn't reached in the first phase, the throughput drops momentarily, down to at most a third of the usual rate, signaling that three round trips — so three phases — were needed to decide instead of just one. The system slows down, but does not grind to a halt.QuePaxa also allows us to confidently switch out which replica acts as leader while the cluster is running. Since the leader isn’t the exclusive driver behind decisions and proposers are cooperative, a temporarily non-optimal leader isn’t as limiting as in other algorithms, where a leader misconfiguration could stall the system completely. We can dynamically tune which proposer is the leader without worrying too much about impacting the stability of a Meerkat cluster.What we’ll be showing nextDesigning Meerkat for a global network forced us to re-evaluate how we approach distributed consensus. Instead of sticking to familiar defaults that didn't quite fit our constraints, we looked to the decades of research produced by academia and industry. That search led us to QuePaxa.Choosing QuePaxa meant choosing a less-traveled path. It has not been battle-tested as extensively as Raft or Paxos, and we’re also extending the original crash-stop design to support crash recovery. This demands careful engineering and stronger evidence of correctness than usual systems.That is why we are formally verifying our QuePaxa implementation and Meerkat as a whole, alongside extensive simulation and fault-injection testing. Future posts in this series will explain how we verify Meerkat and QuePaxa’s Rust implementation, how we test failures that are difficult to reproduce in production, benchmarks, and what we have learned while turning an academic protocol into a production system.Stay on the lookout for further Meerkat updates on the Cloudflare Blog, and if you want to learn more about research at Cloudflare, have a look at our work at Cloudflare Research.

title: [Cloudflare] Launching the Vite Ecosystem Fund
summary: Cloudflare is distributing the first $301,300 of the Vite Ecosystem Fund to 44 projects and maintainers across the Vite ecosystem.When VoidZero joined Cloudflare, we committed $1 million to strengthen the open source ecosystem around Vite. This round is just the start.Sponsoring open source has always mattered, but now AI has made funding urgent.AI is changing open sourceAI has made open source more valuable while triggering more maintainer burnout. Previously, contributing to a project through either an issue or pull request meant you cared about it. In return, maintainers would review and provide feedback. AI changed the social contract of open source. Anyone can now create and submit AI-authored pull requests.The most visible result is the influx of pull requests. As the number of PRs has gone up, the number of maintainers reviewing them has stayed constant. So each maintainer’s workload has grown.During reviews, maintainers often find themselves speaking with an agent and not a person like they used to. If that’s the case, then why not cut out the middleman? Maintainers now have their own agents they can prompt to produce better results since they have more knowledge of the codebase.AI has raised the pressure to produce. It’s made it easier for maintainers to ship features, performance improvements, and bug fixes that would not have been done otherwise. But it’s also made it easy for other projects to do the same. When another project adds overlapping features using AI, maintainers feel a need to keep up using AI. It can become a grinding cycle, where each project pushes the other to move faster. Along the way, some projects have grown in scope and lost sight of their original goals.Maintainer burnout and sustainability have always been a problem — and now AI has accelerated those issues. That’s why sponsoring open source projects and supporting maintainers is so important in this moment.One of the Vite Ecosystem Fund’s first recipients is e18e, a community focused on improving performance across the JavaScript ecosystem. Its lead, James Garbutt, has a long history in open source, and his work at e18e has helped make popular tools like Svelte, Storybook, and Nx faster. "Sponsorships make a huge difference and allow maintainers to dedicate more of their time to the things we all rely on," Garbutt says.Fund distributionThe recipients of the Vite Ecosystem Fund were selected by a panel of core team members from Vite stack projects (Vite, Vitest, Rolldown, Oxc, Vite+), including maintainers not employed by Cloudflare.The funding is allocated through Cloudflare's Open Collective as a combination of:Contributions to ecosystem recipientsStipends to core maintainersWe’re proud that Cloudflare has committed to making the open source ecosystem we rely on stronger and more sustainable. No project thrives in isolation.We'll continue to distribute and draw down the committed amount every quarter.Contributions to ecosystem recipientsThis first round of sponsorships prioritized dependencies, ecosystem critical plugins, significant contributors, and projects that moved the ecosystem forward.Andrew GallantAndrey SitnikAnthony Fu FundAri PerkkiöArtem ZakharchenkoBabelBart WaardenburgBenjamin E. Each maintainer can invoice at a rate of $50 per hour contributed that month.Any time spent improving or supporting the project in some way counts towards this stipend: writing code, writing documentation, triaging issues, offering support in our Discord servers, attending meetings or meetups, contributing to our upstream dependencies, and so on.Maintainers who are already being paid for or employed for this work do not receive stipends — for example, VoidZero employees are ineligible.Cloudflare supports open sourceCloudflare’s mission is to help build a better Internet. These sponsorships are a small thank-you for all this hard work.

title: [Slack Engineering] Shipyard: How We Built Slack’s Next-Generation EC2 Platform
summary: Over the past few years, we’ve been on a journey to modernise how we run Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) instances at Slack. In our first post, Advancing Our Chef Infrastructure, we shared how we moved from a single Chef stack to a resilient, multi-stack setup with versioned cookbook deployments and safer promotion workflows. This afforded us far more reliability and operational control across tens of thousands of EC2 instances. Subsequently, in Advancing Our Chef Infrastructure: Safety Without Disruption, we tackled deployment risk without the need for teams to rewrite their cookbooks. By introducing split production environments, signal-based Chef runs, and smarter rollout mechanisms, we dramatically reduced the impact radius of failures while keeping our legacy platform stable. These changes allowed us to safely operate our EC2 ecosystem at scale while we plan the future at a relaxed pace. But as we kept improving, a bigger truth became clear. Even with safer rollouts, better orchestration, and stronger guardrails, the old model—continuously updating long-lived EC2 instances—was hitting its limits. Service-level deployments were tricky, infrastructure drift was inevitable, and coordinating changes across multiple layers added complexity. Containers solved this for some classes of workloads, but not everything could migrate easily. We needed a new approach—one that brought modern deployment practices like immutability, progressive rollouts, and automated safety directly to EC2 instances. Enter Shipyard. Shipyard is Slack’s next-generation EC2 platform. It treats infrastructure as deployable artifacts rather than endlessly mutable instances. It gives teams service-level deployment primitives, tight integration with our build and orchestration systems, and the confidence to update infrastructure with the same safety and predictability we expect from modern app delivery platforms. In this post—the third chapter of our journey—we’ll explain why we built Shipyard, the principles behind its design, and how it represents a fundamental shift in how we think about running EC2 instances at Slack. What Shipyard Provides Shipyard is designed to bring modern infrastructure principles to EC2 instances while preserving the flexibility teams expect from EC2. Rather than focusing on configuration management as the center of the system, Shipyard shifts responsibility toward build pipelines, deployable artifacts, and automated safety mechanisms. Some of the key capabilities of the platform include: Multi-Architecture and Multi-OS Support The platform is designed from the start to support multiple CPU architectures, including both AMD64 and ARM-based Graviton instances, with support for multiple operating systems such as Ubuntu, RHEL, and Amazon Linux. This flexibility allows teams to optimize for cost, performance, or compatibility without needing separate platform implementations. Shipyard is particularly valuable for workloads that cannot migrate to containers, such as infrastructure components, Kubernetes worker nodes, and our egress network stacks. Metrics-Driven Deployments with Safety Controls Each service integrates with our deployment orchestration system called Gondola to enable progressive rollouts with metric based automated safety checks. Deployments can automatically halt based on service health signals, or automated rollback to previous known good versions. Fast and Predictable Provisioning Shipyard uses a layered image approach, inspired by how containers work. A shared “golden” base image provides common infrastructure components, and service-specific images are built on top of that foundation. This minimizes work at launch time, so instances can come online quickly and predictably across regions. Simplified Configuration Management One of the biggest architectural shifts is how we use configuration management. Previously, instances would run scheduled Chef jobs that periodically checked and reapplied configuration, so any manual or unexpected changes would be reverted back to the desired state. In the new model, configuration is applied during well-defined lifecycle phases like image baking and initial provisioning, rather than being continuously enforced in the background. Configuration tools are mainly used to deploy services, not to constantly modify the entire system. This reduces background load, avoids unintended overwrites, and makes system behavior much easier to reason about, since instances aren’t continuously changing over time. Real-Time Inventory and Fleet Visibility Shipyard comes with a new inventory system called Peekaboo, giving us near real-time visibility into the state of our EC2 fleet. Instead of relying on Chef Server as the source of truth, Peekaboo taps directly into cloud events and instance metadata, providing better telemetry across environments. It can even track instances from non-Shipyard deployments, giving us a complete view of the entire fleet in one place. We built Peekaboo using AWS EventBridge, OpenSearch, and Lambda. It has everything teams need: a UI to explore the fleet, an API for integrations, and a command-line interface (CLI) for quick command-line checks. By centralising this information, it removes the guesswork and gives us a single place to view and manage EC2 instances. Short-Lived, Continuously Refreshed Instances To keep our EC2 instances secure and truly immutable, each instance has a limited lifespan and is automatically rotated on a regular schedule. This means our fleets are always fresh; potential vulnerabilities have less time to cause issues, and teams focus on replacing instances rather than making in-place changes. Golden Base Images: Introducing slack-zero At the foundation of the Shipyard is a shared base image called “slack-zero.” This is the core machine image built by Slack’s Compute Platform Team and maintained collaboratively with our security and monitoring teams. The slack-zero image contains: Operating system baseline and hardening Networking and service discovery configuration Monitoring and security agents Common tooling and foundational system configuration You can think of slack-zero similarly to how teams use a base Docker image or how we start from a vendor-supplied Ubuntu image and layer additional components on top. It provides a standardised, trusted foundation that every service inherits, while still allowing teams to customize their own runtime environment on top of it. Base images are treated as immutable but ephemeral. When foundational components need to change—such as a security patch, monitoring update, or networking improvement—a new slack-zero image is produced. Downstream service images can then rebuild on top of the updated base to inherit the latest fixes and improvements. To build slack-zero, we use AWS Image Builder rather than Packer. Image Builder provides several built-in advantages over our previous approach with Packer, including: Lifecycle Management: Old AMIs are automatically cleaned up using lifecycle policies, helping reduce storage costs. AWS System Manager (SSM) Parameter Publishing: Each new slack-zero image updates an SSM parameter that indicates the latest available AMI for an account. Service pipelines read this parameter to ensure they always build on the most up-to-date base. Event-Driven Automation: When a slack-zero image finishes baking successfully, EventBridge and Lambda automatically trigger downstream pipelines in service owner accounts so dependent images can be rebuilt. Built-in Testing: Before an AMI is published, Image Builder launches temporary instances and runs validation tests. This ensures every image is verified before distribution, reducing risk and increasing confidence in production rollouts. Together, these capabilities allow us to continuously evolve the platform foundation while keeping adoption friction low for service teams. Service Images Each service team builds its own AMIs using slack-zero as the foundation. This allows teams to control their runtime environment while inheriting standardized platform components maintained by the platform organization. Service image pipelines define: What software is installed How the service is configured What happens during instance initialisation for this service Because most configuration is baked directly into the image, instances launch quickly and consistently, minimizing configuration drift and ensuring predictable behavior across the fleet. By combining the immutable slack-zero base with service-specific layers, Shipyard provides both platform stability and team-level flexibility, enabling services to innovate safely without sacrificing operational consistency. Baking and Provisioning Shipyard separates instance preparation into two distinct phases: baking and provisioning. During the bake phase, we install packages and include configuration that is consistent across environments. This ensures every instance starts from a fully prepared, known-good state with the majority of work already completed before launch. Environment-specific settings—such as secrets, regional configuration, or deployment metadata—are applied during the provisioning phase when the instance boots. This step is intentionally lightweight and typically involves only dropping configuration, retrieving secrets, and starting services. By moving heavy operations like package installation into the bake phase, instances can become operational in seconds rather than minutes. This fast startup time is critical for scaling events, rolling deployments, and automated instance replacement. This provisioning model provides a strong balance of consistency, speed, and flexibility: images deliver a stable baseline, while minimal provisioning adapts instances to their runtime environment without introducing drift. Deployments and Fleet Updates When teams need to roll out changes, they build a new Amazon Machine Instance (AMI) and then run their deployment pipeline to roll it out. Instead of patching existing instances, fleets are updated through controlled replacements, keeping everything consistent and predictable. For Auto Scaling Groups (ASGs), we use AWS Instance Refresh, and Kubernetes worker fleets use Karpenter for lifecycle-driven updates. Services with special deployment needs can use alternative rollout executors. Our global deployment orchestrator, Gondola, supports these patterns, giving teams flexibility while keeping a consistent deployment experience. Emergency Fixes and Rapid Deployment Pathways For urgent situations, the platform allows targeted configuration changes on running instances, but these are meant for emergencies only. Affected instances are expected to be replaced afterward via regular deployment pipelines. Our emergency workflows use AWS Systems Manager with a predefined document to run selected Chef recipes, letting teams quickly apply critical fixes. Once stable, instances are cycled to return to the intended immutable state. What Do Customer Pipelines Look Like? Customer pipelines in Shipyard can have multiple stages, giving teams flexibility to design them around their service and operational needs. Each stage in Gondola represents a deployable unit, such as an ASG, a Kubernetes cluster, or a group of EC2 instances. For example, the Egress Team runs separate canary and production ASGs in each availability zone, with deployment stages ordered so updates flow sequentially. Gondola updates each stage, monitors key metrics, and rolls back automatically if problems are detected, preventing issues from spreading. This staged approach, combined with Shipyard’s fast provisioning and immutable AMIs, lets teams safely deploy complex updates at scale while maintaining observability and control. What Happens in the Gondola Stage? When Gondola builds an artifact, it produces a deployable package for a service with two main parts: The AMI to roll out across the fleet The Chef artifact containing versioned recipes associated with a Git commit Gondola treats these together as a single deployable unit. Each stage uses a service-defined executor to perform the rollout: ASG-based deployments: The executor updates the launch template with the new AMI and configuration. Chef code is packaged to Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3), and new instances use a baked-in bootstrapper to fetch the correct artifact and run the relevant recipes. Configuration metadata ensures only the right configuration is applied. Kubernetes worker fleets: The executor tells Karpenter which AMI to use and provides the same configuration metadata. Nodes bootstrap in the same way, ensuring consistent provisioning. For services with special deployment needs, Gondola makes it easy to add new executors. This lets Shipyard support different deployment models while keeping artifact handling and provisioning consistent and predictable. By combining AMI updates, versioned configuration artifacts, and metadata-driven bootstrapping, Gondola ensures every instance gets the correct software and configuration for its role, no matter how it’s deployed. Simple Pipeline Shared Responsibility Shipyard’s layered image model is built on a clear shared responsibility between platform teams and service teams. The Compute, Security, and Monitoring teams manage the base layer, making sure it includes all global infrastructure components, security patches, and essential configurations. Service teams then build their own AMIs on top of this base, adding the software and settings specific to their service. Whenever the Compute team rolls out a fix or update—whether it’s a security patch, a monitoring agent update, or a networking change—service teams are responsible for incorporating the updated base into their own AMIs. This way, every service image automatically benefits from the latest improvements and security fixes from the shared base. This approach lets each team focus on what they do best while keeping the fleet consistent, secure, and reliable. The diagram below illustrates how the base and service layers work together and highlights where each team’s responsibilities lie. A Caveat on Immutability While Shipyard instances are mostly immutable, there is an important exception: secrets. Each instance runs the Consul Template service, which allows us to roll out updated secrets from Vault without cycling the fleet. This means that, although packages and configurations are fixed at bake time, sensitive data like credentials or certificates can still be updated dynamically. Our infrastructure is semi-immutable: the core system and service layers remain consistent, but critical runtime secrets can be refreshed safely as needed. This approach balances stability, predictability, and security across the fleet. The Reaper The Reaper evaluates two primary inputs. First, it consumes signals from external systems—such as security tooling or AWS EC2 events—that indicate an instance may no longer be in its desired state and should be considered “tainted.” Second, The Reaper performs periodic checks to identify instances that have been running for longer than their allowed lifespan. When either condition is met, the instance is scheduled for replacement according to its service policies. This approach helps reduce configuration drift, limit exposure to vulnerabilities, and reinforce the principle that infrastructure should be updated by redeploying rather than modifying systems in place. The result is a platform that is more reliable, auditable, and predictable. For example, while manual remote access remains available for emergency scenarios, manually accessing a production-class node will generate a signal that marks the instance for eventual replacement, supporting our immutable infrastructure goals. The Reaper also integrates with Peekaboo to track instance age across the fleet. Once a node reaches its maximum lifespan, it follows the same graceful replacement workflow. Looking ahead, we plan to make the system more context-aware so that only meaningful changes—such as software updates or configuration drift—trigger replacement, while read-only or low-risk actions do not create unnecessary churn. Taming the Reaper The Reaper is designed not only to enforce lifecycle policies, but also to give teams control over how replacements occur. Built-in rate limiting allows service owners to define how many instances can be replaced at a time, scoped by service, region, or availability zone, preventing sudden capacity impacts. For emergency situations, we provide a global pause mechanism—the “big red button.” By placing a control object in S3, teams can temporarily halt all Reaper activity across the fleet. This provides a safe and immediate way to stop instance cycling during incidents or periods of elevated risk. We also provide a CLI that allows service owners to manage rate limits, inspect configuration, and activate or release the global pause when needed. In addition, controlled access mechanisms such as short-lived SSH certificate workflows can be used for break-glass scenarios where deeper investigation is required, while still maintaining overall lifecycle safety commitments. Together, these capabilities make the Reaper both predictable and controllable—enforcing instance immutability by default while giving teams the visibility and safeguards they need to operate confidently. How Do We Test Changes? Both platform teams and service owners need a safe way to test cookbook changes before merging a pull request, so we built a system called Ship Quick—a developer workflow that runs a realistic bake-and-provision test on real infrastructure. Developers run a CLI command from their cookbook repo, where a YAML file defines the test cases. Ship Quick packages the cookbook, uploads it to S3, and sends a workflow message to a queue. A fleet of worker instances—managed by a lightweight process called Longshoremen—picks up the job, detaches from its Auto Scaling Group, runs the Chef workflow, streams logs back to the CLI, and then terminates (unless the developer chooses to keep it for debugging). We run Longshorem in two separate worker fleets because of how our bootstrapping works. The vanilla Ubuntu fleet is used to bake and test the base slack-zero image—it can’t build on top of itself, so starting from a clean Ubuntu AMI is required. The slack-zero fleet is for service team cookbooks, which depend on the pre-baked slack-zero AMI. Running tests from this fleet ensures provisioning is validated against the same foundation used in production. Splitting the fleets this way helps ensure each layer is tested against the correct base. Both fleets scale automatically with demand, and slack-zero workers are continuously updated to the latest images so tests always reflect the current production environment. Teams that build images in their own AWS accounts can also provision dedicated worker fleets and route Ship Quick jobs to them, ensuring isolation while keeping the same workflow. What’s Next? So far, Shipyard has been working really well for short-lived services, and we’re actively onboarding teams from the legacy EC2 platform. Our next challenge is long-lived instances—things like Slack’s data nodes, singleton services like GitHub Enterprise, or third-party business technology instances such as Atlassian JIRA. These can’t be cycled quickly, so we need ways to patch and update them safely while ensuring the Reaper handles them correctly. We’re collaborating closely with service teams to develop new deploy executors in Gondola for these longer-lived workloads. As more teams adopt Shipyard, we’ll keep iterating on tooling, developer workflows, and the overall deployment experience to meet the platform’s diverse needs. Future posts in this series will cover the challenges we encounter as Shipyard evolves and take a closer look at its components—including the Shipyard API, image pipelines, developer workflows, and our inventory system. Stay tuned!

title: [Dropbox Tech] How AI-assisted development helped us build the new Dropbox experience
summary: For three years, we’ve been working toward a new Dropbox experience that helps people do more with their files, from finding a project decision to getting a folder ready to share. Today, we’re beginning to roll that experience out to customers. But getting here meant changing how we build software. We had complex integrations to tackle and a deadline to meet, and AI-assisted development helped us take on work that would've previously been difficult to complete in time for launch. The new Dropbox experience puts that investment into practice by helping customers understand what’s in their files and get work done with them. Ask Dropbox what changed in a project folder, and it answers with sources you can open and check. Ask it to organize a folder, rename files based on their contents, or combine documents into a PDF, and it shows a plan you can review and edit before approving. Dropbox only reads and acts on content you already have permission to access, and supported file changes can be undone. And the results stay in Dropbox, where teams can review, share, and keep working with them. Delivering that experience meant building new capabilities on web and bringing them into desktop, with shared code that let us develop features for both applications. Engineers took broader ownership of product decisions and brought quality checks into development from the start. As the work progressed, we moved from using AI to help with individual coding steps to delegating defined tasks—including implementation and testing—for engineers to review. Together, those changes helped us deliver a product years in the making within an ambitious launch timeline. Bringing more of Dropbox into desktop We began with a broad product direction and a lot of details to work out. We needed to turn that direction into specific experiences people could use, including a fuller desktop app. Desktop had primarily focused on keeping files in sync, while web already supported richer ways to browse and work with content. We wanted to build on that foundation and bring both existing features and new capabilities developed on web into desktop without rebuilding everything separately for each platform. The difficulty was that web and desktop had grown around different needs. They used different tools to build and release software and handled tasks such as signing in, navigating between pages, and retrieving data differently. A web feature could depend on services that desktop didn’t provide in the same way. Before we could reuse it, engineers needed to identify those dependencies and work out how to support them—a substantial integration effort to complete before our November launch deadline. During our Hackathon in May, engineers built a working prototype that explored two possible approaches to tackling this problem, and AI helped them trace dependencies, identify platform-specific assumptions, and test the integration. One approach displayed the existing All Files page inside a desktop-specific window using Electron, the framework behind desktop’s interface. An embedded web view—a browser surface inside the app—let us bring the existing web browsing experience into desktop quickly. The second approach imported selected web components directly into desktop’s user interface. These individual building blocks required more integration work but gave us greater control over how they fit into the desktop app. The working prototype gave Product and Design something concrete to try before we committed to a larger architectural change. Engineers turned directional designs into usable flows, surfaced missing states, and proposed options as platform constraints became clear. Product and Design worked through those choices as engineers built the features, allowing us to refine the experience as we learned. We found that both approaches had a place: complete web pages where we wanted close parity, and individual components where we needed more control. AI reduced the effort of testing those options, helping turn a long-standing product direction into an early version of the desktop experience we developed for launch. Alongside the desktop work, engineers used coding agents to implement defined interface changes across Home, Library, and file previews. These included the Jump Back In list view and grid-to-list toggle, giving people another way to browse and return to their work. Agents also handled smaller updates to menus, upload banners, and shared styling. Handing off those tasks gave engineers more time to focus on how the product should behave and how the experiences should connect. That combination helped us move the broader desktop experience and its individual interface improvements toward launch. Building capabilities that can work across platforms The prototype showed that we could bring more of the web experience into desktop. Next, we needed a way to keep improving both applications without rebuilding the same features twice. We wanted Dropbox to feel familiar whether someone used it on web or desktop. That meant reusing the code that makes a feature look and work the same in both places, while letting each app handle things like signing in and moving between screens in its own way. We share React components—the pieces of code that build what people see and interact with—along with the code they need to work with data. Web and desktop each build and test those components as part of their own app. When a shared feature needs information, it asks for it in the same way on either platform. Web handles that request through the browser, while desktop uses its own networking system. That lets us reuse the feature without making both apps work exactly the same way behind the scenes. Engineers had to work out which code could be reused and which parts needed to work differently in each app. AI helped them follow the connections between those pieces, pull out reusable components, and write adapters—the code that connects a shared feature to each app’s services—along with tests. Engineers reviewed the resulting code to check that it worked as intended. AI helped us complete that integration before launch, putting an approach we had discussed for years into practice. Now, improvements to shared features have a path to both web and desktop. Making the new experience usable by more people The new capabilities also needed to work for people using a keyboard, a screen reader, or an enlarged display. As we prepared for launch, engineers used AI-assisted development to deliver 22 accessibility features across Home, All Files, file previews, and Photos. These included announcements that help screen-reader users follow changes in the Up Next carousel on web and desktop, and improvements to navigating the All Files table. The team also fixed how keyboard focus moves between controls and adjusted layouts to keep pages usable at 200%–400% zoom. To carry out this work, the web team gave coding agents clearly defined tasks and a consistent process to follow. Each task started with a written plan agreed on by the engineer and agent. The agent made the changes, ran the relevant builds and tests locally, and recorded the results for an engineer to review before accepting the code. Instructions stored with the code explained the rules agents needed to follow, giving engineers a repeatable way to delegate work while remaining responsible for the result. A working group and champions across teams helped establish those shared instructions, task formats, and review expectations, so the approach could be used consistently across the project. Retiring an older file list had been deferred for two quarters because updating the automated tests required substantial engineering time. AI-assisted development gave the team a practical way to tackle that cleanup alongside its launch work. Engineers divided the cleanup into 53 tasks. Coding agents then updated or removed the affected tests using the same testing and review process, and the team finished all of those tasks in one week. The team also used coding agents to add automated tests for five core parts of the web app, including the file browser people use to navigate their content. By checking for problems when the code changes, these tests help engineers catch issues before they reach customers. Beyond writing tests, AI agents tried out the experience during development, which helped engineers catch problems while they were still working on the relevant code. In one case, an agent found that a deleted item in Chat history could remain visible until the page was refreshed; engineers fixed the underlying synchronization issue and added tests to prevent it from returning. This let human reviewers spend more time assessing whether the experience made sense to customers, while automated checks helped catch functional problems. And importantly, customer feedback helped us decide what to improve and when to expand access. All eight of our initial design partners chose to keep the new experience enabled. As we introduced the experience to larger groups, we watched how people used familiar features such as upload, preview, search, and sharing, and tracked whether AI actions succeeded and whether customers switched the experience off. Those signals helped us prioritize issues, while the coding-agent workflow gave engineers a consistent way to implement and check fixes. AI helped us work through the changes; customer feedback and engineering review guided what was ready to reach more people. A foundation for what comes next The new Dropbox experience reflects years of work toward helping customers understand their content and complete more of the tasks around it. AI-assisted development helped us bring that direction to launch by making it easier to test a fuller desktop experience, connect features across web and desktop, and address accessibility and testing work while building new capabilities. Engineers guided that work, deciding how the applications should fit together and checking the changes against the behaviors customers depend on. The value of that work extends beyond this release. Shared components let improvements reach both applications. And the process engineers used to delegate and review accessibility fixes and testing work gives them a way to tackle further improvements, with customer feedback helping determine where to focus. Together, these practices give us more room to improve Dropbox as we learn how people use it. They also broaden the work engineers can take on: understanding customer needs, trying out interactions, weighing product decisions, and following changes through release. Technical expertise remains essential, and AI gives engineers more opportunities to apply it across those responsibilities. Their judgment and customers’ needs continue to guide what we build and why. ~ ~ ~ If building innovative products, experiences, and infrastructure excites you, come build the future with us!
